transcript: When I saw that Paul Giamatti, John Turturro, Tatiana Maslany were all starring in a play together, I knew I had to make the trip up to Boston to check it out. The play is called rhinoceros, and it's very strange. The plot is basically this scene from Amazing Spider Man “I am the rhino!” where everyday people, including Paul Giamatti, start turning into rhinoceroses. What exactly is causing this is not clear, nor is it ever explained, but it does seem to be at least somewhat voluntary, and the play uses this to explore ideas of conformity. And in this case, conforming literally means giving up your humanity in order to become a rhinoceros like everyone else. And given that description, it's probably not too hard to see the parallels to today's society, as the metaphor is not exactly subtle. And despite this play being over 60 years old, there were quite a few moments that felt surprisingly timely and like they could have been written yesterday. Now this is not a review, so I don't wanna get too deep into analysis. I'll probably do that in a separate video. But I will say one of the main reasons to see this production is for Paul Giamatti's absolutely unhinged performance towards the end of Act 1 where he, yes, turns into a rhinoceros. “I am the rhino!” No one in the show ever dresses up as a rhinoceros, and anytime a rhinoceros is seen, it's always off stage. So He does this transformation scene purely through his own physicality. And it might just be my favourite individual scene of theatre that I have seen all year. And if it ever comes to New York, I think that he could win a Tony for this scene alone. It is truly that good. And I think that this show is at its best when it is fully leaning into the absurdity, when the actors are let off their leash and just allowed to get really wild with it. Because at the end of the day, it's a play about people turning into rhinoceroses, Okay, it's inherently silly, but underneath that is a surprisingly poignant message that still resonates even 60+ years later.
